disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation) is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention—such as disorganization, distractibility, and forgetfulness—without the prominent overt hyperactivity seen in the combined type. Symptoms must begin in childhood, be present in at least two settings, persist for at least six months, and cause clinically significant impairment in social, academic, or occupational functioning. In adults, it often presents as chronic difficulties with planning, sustaining focus on tasks, managing time, and following through, rather than overt behavioral disruption. It can be misattributed to anxiety, depression, or personality traits, so course since childhood, pervasiveness across contexts, and a longstanding history of similar difficulties help distinguish it from other conditions or purely situational stress reactions.

narrative.personality: A reserved, detail‑oriented rural family physician, David is disciplined and work‑centered yet prone to quiet worry and solitary, perfectionistic pursuits like fly‑fishing and woodworking.
narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, David’s small rural clinic transitioned to a new electronic health record system while simultaneously expanding telemedicine services, dramatically increasing the volume of digital paperwork, protocols, and remote visits he was expected to juggle. He had always coped with lifelong distractibility by relying on paper charts, handwritten lists, and long hours, but the rapid shift to multiple digital platforms and constant on‑screen alerts exposed how much he struggled to keep track of tasks and maintain steady focus during prolonged sessions. Over the following year, he found himself staying later and later to finish notes, missing follow‑ups he had meant to schedule, and feeling uncharacteristically restless in long meetings and case conferences, which began to affect his reputation among colleagues and his confidence in his own reliability. When his medical director gently raised concerns about his increasing inefficiency and David’s wife commented on how preoccupied and agitated he seemed even at home, he agreed to seek a psychiatric evaluation to understand why he suddenly felt unable to stay seated and on task in settings that had never bothered him before.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to sit through meetings or finish my charting without getting up and pacing around.”

narrative.personality: Maria is a competitive, routine‑loving teen who pours her energy into cooking, sports, and gaming, but often finds herself scattered and disorganized when life gets busy.
narrative.stressor: During her junior year of high school, Maria’s class schedule became more demanding just as she started taking on extra responsibilities at home and volunteering at the Honduran cultural center, leaving her with little structure or support for her schoolwork. She had long relied on her competitiveness and love of routine to get by despite a childhood history of being easily sidetracked in class, but the increasing need to sit still for longer lessons, standardized test prep, and online assignments made it much harder for her to stay in one place and follow through. Over the next year, she began skipping portions of classes by stepping out frequently, falling behind on coursework, and ultimately failing several subjects, which led to her leaving school without a diploma and feeling ashamed and frustrated that she could not seem to “just focus” like her peers. As her dreams of working in a professional kitchen started to feel out of reach and teachers and family members criticized her for not trying hard enough, a school counselor suggested an evaluation, prompting Maria to see a psychiatrist because she felt unable to remain seated and engaged in any structured learning environment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t stay in my seat at school or during anything that’s supposed to be sit‑down, I keep getting up even when I know I shouldn’t.”

narrative.personality: Lazaro is a hyper‑organized, curiosity‑driven community organizer who loves art and learning but is prone to intense anxiety and occasional impulsive splurges on creative projects.
narrative.stressor: After finishing high school and attempting a few part‑time jobs, Lazaro decided to focus on building art‑driven community projects and exploring further education options, moving from the clear structure of school into a self‑directed schedule. Without the external deadlines and daily routines that had previously masked his lifelong tendency to drift off during mentally demanding tasks, he suddenly had to generate his own sustained focus for grant applications, long‑form reading, and planning complex events. Over the next year, he noticed that while he could spend hours on photography or cooking, he repeatedly put off paperwork, avoided dense reading related to mental‑health programming, and hopped between ideas instead of pushing through the more cognitively demanding parts of his projects, leading to missed opportunities and stalled initiatives. Feeling frustrated that his carefully designed Trello boards and planning rituals still weren’t enough to help him sit with sustained mental effort, and worried that this pattern was holding back both his career and his community work, he sought a psychiatric evaluation to understand why he kept dodging any task that required prolonged concentration.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Any time I have to sit and really concentrate on something for a while, I end up avoiding it or bouncing away from it.”
